## SURVEY OF CRIME ## I.P.C. Crimes 9,55,422 Cognizable Crimes under the Indian Penal Code were reported in India during 1970 showing an increase of 13.0% over 1969. This figure includes crimes committed by Juveniles. The trend of crime during the sixties shows a rise till the year 1967, except for marginal decreases in 1963 and 1965. There was a decrease from 1967 to 1969 and during 1970 there has been a very sharp increase.

## SURVEY OF CRIME ## I.P.C. Crimes During the calendar year 1969, a total number of 8,45,167 Cognizable Crimes under the Indian Penal Code was reported in India showing a decrease of 2·0% over 1968. This figure includes crimes committed by Juveniles. The trend of crime during the sixties shows a rise till the year 1967 except for marginal decreases in 1963 and 1965 and a decrease thereafter.

109 ## Disposal of Juveniles 5.8. A total of 1,50,212 juveniles were sent to the Courts during 1983. Cases in respect of 46.0 per cent of the total number of juveniles sent to courts remained pending for disposal at the end of the year. As compared to 1982, the pendency of disposal of juveniles registered a decline of 4.4 per cent during 1983 as the pendency of cases decreased from 72,279 in 1982 to 69,110 in 1983. During the year 1983, 27.0 per cent of the juveniles whose cases were sent to the Courts for disposal were either acquitted or otherwise disposed of in comparison to 18.8 per cent in 1982. The relevant statistics are set forth in Table-44. Of the 1,50,212 Juveniles sent to court during 1983, 8.6 per cent were restored to guardians, 1.8 per cent were placed on probation, 0.3 per cent were sent to Reformatories and Borstals, 1.1 per cent were sent to schools and institutions, 1.1 per cent were sent to adult institutions, 14.1 per cent were imprisoned, 27.0 per cent were acquitted or otherwise disposed of and cases in respect of 46.0 per cent of them were pending.

119 The phenomenon of urban crimes is an important feature in metropolitan cities but the pattern varies from city to city. 2.3.2 India is predominantly a rural country as only 25.7 per cent of its population lives in urban areas (as per 1991 census) while majority of the population(74.3%) lives in rural areas. Of the total Urban population (2,171.8 lakhs), nearly one-third (769.9 lakhs) constituting 35.44 per cent live in 23 metropolitan cities (one million plus population). The proportion of metropolitan cities population to the national population is 8.7 per cent. There is no demarcation between rural and urban areas as far as the crime statistics are concerned since these were not collected on this basis, but as the crimes in urban areas are peculiar and have shown a consistent rise parallel to the population increase, during the previous few decades, it has generated interest to make a study of the crime phenomenon. An attempt has been made to highlight the prevalence of some crimes in the Urban areas. For the sake of analysis of crime situation in these areas we have confined ourselves with the available data of above mentioned 23 Metropolitan Cities only.

CHAPTER 7 PREMISES OF DACOITY AND ROBBERY The cases registered under 'Dacoity' and 'Robbery' in the country were further analysed according to the place of occurrence of these two crimes. The highest number of Dacoity cases (10,801) were committed in residential premises and only four cases on 'Rivers and at Sea' were reported out of 14,590 total cases in 1981. The highest number of 'Robbery cases (7,859) were committed in residential premises, followed by 'Robbery on high-ways' (3.504) and only 18 cases of 'Robbery on Rivers and at Sea' and 19 cases of 'Robbery in Banks' were reported during 1981. In Delhi the majority of robberies were committed in residential premises followed by commercial establishments. The relevant statistics are set forth in Table-50 and 51.

CHAPTER 9 RECIDIVISM 9.1 The information on 'Recidivism' was available in respect of 21,80,573 offenders during the year 1986 out of which 19,29,431 i.e., 88.5% were new offenders. The percentage of persons who were convicted once, twice and thrice or more was 9.0%, 1.6% and 0.9% respectively. It was found that 17.7% of the persons arrested for the offence of 'Burglary' were convicted in the past and this accounted for the highest percentage of 'Recidivism' closely followed by 'Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder' (17.0%), 'Theft' (16.0%) and 'Dacoity' (14.9%). The relevant statistics in respect of number of offenders and their percentage distribution of 'Recidivism' are presented in Tables 53 and 54. Crimes under the Special and Local Laws (SLL) 1 18.1 The crime head-wise incidence and rate of cognizable crimes under the Special and Local Laws (SLL) during 1987 and 1992 to 1996 are presented in Table-10. The quinquennial average of incidence and rate for the period 1992-96 as also the percentage variations during 1997 over 1987, Q.A. and over the previous year (1996) are also presented in this table. 1.18.2 During 1997, a total of 46,91,439 cognizable crimes were reported in the country under various Special Laws and Local Laws. These incidents showed a steady increase, with 30.7 per cent over the decade 1987-97, 15.6 per cent over the Q.A. of 1992-96 and 2.3 per cent over the previous year (1996). 1.18.3 The crime head-wise percentage distribution of various cognizable crimes under the SLL during the last 5 years (1952 to 1996) is presented in Table-11. It is observed that the 21 specified crimes heads accounted for one-fifth (21.4%) of the total SLL crimes, while the remaining 78.6 per cent were clubbed as “Over SLL crimes”. The “Prohibition Act” and “Excise Act”, though enforced in only a few States, were a major contributor with 14.0 per cent have toward and SLL crimes. Next in order were the “Gambling Act” (2.5%) and the “Arms Act” (1.6%). Each of the remaining 17 specified crimes contributed less than 1 per cent and together accounted for the 2.3 per cent of the total SLL crimes. N.C.R.B., (M.H.A.) CRIME IN INDIA - 1994 17.5.4 The above figures which include baggage seizures, demonstrate that there has been a fall in the smuggling of precious metals over the years since 1991. The quantity of gold smuggled in has also fallen from 5596 kgs in 1990 to 1147 kgs in 1994. Similar is the case with silver which recorded 220318 kgs in 1990 and dwindled to 6404 kgs in 1994. The goods such as synthetic fibres, diamonds also recorded a considerable fall. One contributing factor could be the liberalised import policy in the context of liberalisation of the economy adopted in the present decade. 'Narcotic Drugs' are, however, found to be in the priority list of smuggling in 1994 compared to the previous years. There has been a sharp increase of around 350 percent (from 15.8 crores in 1993 to 54.3 crores in 1994) in the value of the 'Drugs' seized by the customs. Electronic goods also seem to be much sought after items for smuggling in 1994 because of perceived premium and the value of the seized articles accounting to Rs. 37.2 crores compared to Rs.35.8 crores in 1993.
